14950: The word spell as a noun has two main meanings. They are quite different from each other, so let's take them one at a time.
Meaning 1: A magical formula or enchantment

A spell is a set of words, phrases, gestures, or rituals believed to have magical power — power to make something happen through supernatural means.

Think of a witch in a fairy tale saying certain words to turn a prince into a frog. That act — those words, that ritual — is a spell. The core idea is: say or do the right thing, and magic is unleashed. Spells appear everywhere in folklore, mythology, and fantasy — from ancient charms scratched onto stones to Hogwarts classrooms.

Spells can be:

  • Helpful — a healing spell, a protection charm, a love spell
  • Harmful — a curse or hex cast on an enemy
  • Transformative or neutral — a spell that makes someone sleep, invisible, or frozen in place

Key phrases using this meaning:

Cast a spell on someone — to use magic on them.
"The sorceress cast a spell on the entire kingdom."

Be under a spell — to be magically controlled or enchanted, often unable to think or act freely.
"He was under a spell and could not leave the forest."

Break a spell — to end or undo the magic.
"The spell was broken the moment she spoke his true name."

The figurative use (non-magical contexts)

This is important: in everyday modern language, "spell" is often used figuratively — meaning there is no actual magic, but something or someone has such a powerful, almost enchanting hold over a person that the word "spell" feels right.

"The music cast a spell over the whole room."
"She was completely under his spell."

Here, the speaker doesn't literally mean magic. They mean: the effect was so powerful, so captivating, that it felt magical. This figurative use is very common.

This is also where the word spellbound comes from. If someone is spellbound, they are so completely fascinated or captivated that they can barely move or speak — as though frozen by a magical spell.

"The children sat spellbound as the storyteller painted pictures with her words."

Entirely separate from magic, a spell can simply mean a stretch or period of time — usually a temporary one that comes and then passes.

"We had a cold spell last week." — a stretch of cold days
"He went through a rough spell after losing his job." — a difficult period
"There was a quiet spell in the middle of the storm." — a brief calm phase

Notice the pattern: a spell suggests something that lasts for a while but eventually ends. You'd use it for phases, bouts, or episodes — not for something permanent. A city that is rainy year-round doesn't have a "rainy spell"; a city that gets unexpectedly heavy rain for two weeks does.

Used for health episodes

One of the most common uses of this meaning is for brief physical episodes:

  • A dizzy spell — a short bout of dizziness
  • A fainting spell — a brief episode of losing consciousness
  • A coughing spell — a sudden, intense stretch of coughing
  • A sick spell / a bad spell — a period of feeling unwell

These all describe something that hits you for a while and then passes.

Used to mean "a while"

Especially in informal and regional English (particularly in parts of the United States), a spell can simply mean "a while" or "some time."

"Come sit with us for a spell." — Come sit with us for a while.
"I haven't seen him in quite a spell." — I haven't seen him in quite some time.
"She rested for a spell before continuing." — She rested briefly before going on.

This usage is casual, warm, and often carries a slightly old-fashioned or rural feel.
Meaning 3: A turn of work (less common, older)

There is a third, older meaning you may encounter in older books or certain dialects: a spell can mean a turn at doing a task, especially to relieve another person who has been doing it.

"Let me take a spell at the oars." — Let me row for a while so you can rest.
"They each took a spell at the pump." — They each took turns working the pump.

The idea is: you do it for a stretch, then someone else takes over. This meaning is rare in modern everyday speech but you'll see it in historical texts or literature.

—What it meansExample

Spell (noun) — three senses:

1. Magic/enchantment — Words, rituals, or acts believed to have magical power; also used figuratively to describe any powerful, captivating influence. Related: cast a spell, under a spell, break a spell, spellbound.

2. A period of time — A stretch of time, usually temporary. Used for weather patterns, health episodes (dizzy spell, fainting spell), difficult phases, and informally to mean "a while."

3. A turn of work (older/less common) — Taking over a task from someone else for a stretch so they can rest.

The two meanings you'll encounter most often in modern life are the magic sense (including its figurative use) and the period of time sense — especially in phrases like "a cold spell," "a dizzy spell," and "stay for a spell." Knowing both, and recognizing the figurative extension of the magic sense, will cover virtually every use of this word you'll ever come across.
14951:
The verb spell means to say or write the individual letters of a word in their correct order.

When you spell a word, you are breaking it down into its letters and presenting those letters one by one, either by saying them aloud or writing them out.

Examples:

  • "Can you spell your last name for me?"
  • "She spelled the word slowly: C-O-U-R-A-G-E."
  • "I always spell 'necessary' wrong."
  • "The teacher asked the student to spell 'environment' on the board."

This is the meaning most people know first — it's what you do in a spelling test.

Notice that spelling is not the same as saying a word. When you say a word, you produce the sound. When you spell it, you announce each letter individually.

If someone says "How do you say that word?", they want the sound.
If someone says "How do you spell that word?", they want the letters.

This distinction matters because in English, words are often pronounced very differently from how they look. So spelling a word becomes a separate, important skill — and that's why the verb spell exists independently.
Meaning #2 — To Mean or Lead To (Something)

This is the second major meaning, and it's quite different from the first. Here, spell means to signify, to amount to, or to result in something — usually something serious or bad.

You are essentially saying: "This thing means that outcome is coming."

Examples:

  • "One small mistake could spell disaster."
  • "The storm spelled the end of their camping trip."
  • "Rising costs are spelling trouble for small businesses."
  • "His careless attitude spells danger for the whole team."

The key feeling here: When something spells a consequence, it guarantees or points directly toward that consequence. There's a sense of inevitability — like a warning sign that tells you exactly what's about to happen.

This meaning is almost always used with negative or dramatic outcomes: disaster, trouble, danger, the end, ruin, doom. You would almost never hear "This spells success" — though it's grammatically possible, it sounds unusual. The word naturally pairs with outcomes that feel serious or final.

When you add out to spell, you create a phrasal verb — spell out — which has two related uses.

Use A: To explain something in complete, clear detail — leaving nothing assumed.

This is the most common use of spell out. When you spell something out, you are not being vague. You are saying every part of it explicitly, as if the other person needs everything made obvious.

  • "Do I have to spell it out for you? I want you to leave."
  • "The contract spells out exactly what both parties must do."
  • "Let me spell out the plan step by step."
  • "The manual spells out the safety rules in great detail."

The phrase carries a slight edge of impatience when used in conversation — as if the speaker is frustrated that the other person hasn't understood something that seems obvious. But it can also be neutral, simply meaning "to state clearly."

Use B: To say each letter individually (the literal sense).

  • "Please spell out your full name for the form."
  • "The receptionist asked her to spell out the street name."

This use is just a more emphatic version of the basic meaning — it emphasizes going letter by letter, usually to make sure there is no confusion.
Meaning #4 — To Take Someone's Place (Less Common)

There is a fourth, older meaning of spell that you may come across, though it is not very common in everyday modern English.

To spell someone means to relieve them from a task temporarily — to take over for them so they can rest.

  • "You've been driving for hours. Let me spell you for a while."
  • "She spelled her colleague at the front desk during lunch."

This use is more common in certain regional dialects and older writing. You are unlikely to hear it often in conversation today, but it appears in literature and in some professional contexts (especially in jobs involving long, continuous tasks like long-haul driving, security shifts, or caregiving).

English has two accepted past tense forms for spell, and both are correct — the choice often depends on where you are from.

  • Spelled is the standard form in American English.
  • Spelt is used in British English, though spelled is also accepted there.
FormExample
PresentI spell, she spells
PastI spelled / I spelt
Past participleI have spelled / I have spelt
Present participleI am spelling

Present: "I spell," "She spells every word correctly."
Past (American English): "He spelled it wrong."
Past (British English): "He spelt it wrong."
Past participle: "She has spelled/spelt the word correctly every time."
Present participle / ongoing action: "He is spelling out the instructions carefully."

Both spelled and spelt are correct — neither is a mistake. Use spelled if you're writing for an American audience, and either form for British contexts.
Putting It All Together — A Quick Summary

The verb spell has four main uses:

  1. Name the letters of a word — the everyday meaning: "Spell your name."
  2. Mean or lead to a serious outcome — usually bad: "This spells disaster."
  3. Spell out — explain clearly and completely: "Spell out what you want." (Or, literally, say each letter: "Spell out your address.")
  4. Take over for someone temporarily — older/less common: "Let me spell you."

The first two meanings are the most important ones to master. If you can use spell confidently in a spelling context and in a "this spells trouble" context, you have a strong grip on this word. The phrasal verb spell out is also very useful in everyday conversation and professional writing.
14952:
When something is spellbinding, it is so fascinating and captivating that it completely takes over your attention — as if you are under a magic spell and simply cannot look away, stop listening, or think about anything else.

It is not a mild word. It does not just mean "interesting" or "enjoyable." It means your mind is locked in, totally absorbed, almost helplessly so.

Think about what a spell does in a fairy tale or a fantasy story. A wizard casts a spell on someone, and that person freezes. They are held in place. They cannot move freely. The spell has control over them.

Now replace "magic" with "fascination."

When something is spellbinding, it does the same thing to your attention. It holds you. You lose track of time. You forget where you are. You forget everything else happening around you. The experience — whatever it is — has taken complete control of your focus. That is the power the word carries.

The word also carries a feeling of wonder and enchantment. Being spellbound doesn't feel unpleasant — it feels amazing. You want to stay locked in. You don't want it to end.
What Can Be Described as Spellbinding?

Almost anything that can hold a person's complete, absorbed attention:

  • A performance — a concert, a play, a dance, a speech
  • A story — a novel, a film, a TV show, a documentary
  • A natural sight — a sunset, a storm, a vast landscape
  • A person — someone with an extraordinary presence, charisma, or talent
  • An experience — a magic show, a piece of music, an art exhibition

"Her performance was spellbinding — the entire audience sat in silence, almost afraid to breathe."
"I started watching the documentary at 8 PM and finished it at midnight without realizing the time had passed. It was spellbinding."
"He was a spellbinding speaker. The moment he began talking, the room went completely still."
"We stood at the edge of the canyon, speechless. The view was spellbinding."

It is a word of high praise. Using it means you are not saying something is merely good, or nice, or worth seeing. You are saying it is extraordinary — that it has the rare power to make a person forget the world around them.

Think of it on a scale:

Interesting → Fascinating → Captivating → Spellbinding

Each step up means stronger, deeper, more powerful absorption. "Spellbinding" sits near the top of that scale.
How It Feels to Experience Something Spellbinding

Here are the kinds of things you might feel or notice when you experience something spellbinding:

  • Time seems to disappear. An hour feels like five minutes.
  • You stop noticing things around you — noise, other people, even hunger.
  • You feel a kind of awe, wonder, or electricity.
  • When it ends, you feel almost startled — like waking from a dream.
  • You want to experience it again, or you feel reluctant to leave it.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but not identical:

  • Interesting — it gets your attention, but you can still look away easily. Much weaker than spellbinding.
  • Fascinating — stronger than interesting. It pulls your attention in, but still doesn't fully capture the sense of being held or locked in.
  • Captivating — very close to spellbinding. It holds you. But "captivating" is slightly gentler and doesn't carry quite the same magical intensity.
  • Mesmerizing — very close to spellbinding. It focuses more on a trance-like, almost hypnotic quality — like you are staring without blinking.
  • Riveting — means so gripping that you cannot pull yourself away. Very similar in intensity, but "riveting" often leans more toward suspense and excitement, while "spellbinding" leans more toward wonder and enchantment.

Among all of these, spellbinding is the one that feels most magical — the most enchanted, the most overwhelmingly absorbing.

• It does not simply mean "very good." A meal can be very good without being spellbinding. The word specifically refers to the grip on your attention, not just general quality.
  • It does not mean something scary or overwhelming in a bad way. It is always used positively.
  • It does not apply to small or ordinary things. You wouldn't call a good cup of coffee "spellbinding." The word is reserved for experiences that are genuinely extraordinary in their power to absorb you.
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

Spellbinding describes something so extraordinary and captivating that it holds your attention completely — like a magic spell — making you forget everything else and filling you with a sense of wonder.
14953:
When someone is spellbound, they are so completely fascinated and captivated by something that the rest of the world seems to disappear. Their full attention — mind, eyes, and feelings — is locked onto one thing, and they cannot look away or think about anything else. It is a state of total, helpless, pleasurable absorption.

Think of a child watching a magician pull a rabbit from a hat. Their mouth is slightly open. They have forgotten they were hungry five minutes ago. They are not thinking about school tomorrow. They are just there, 100%, hooked. That child is spellbound.
The Idea Hidden Inside the Word

The word contains the word spell — as in a magic spell. Imagine a wizard casting a spell on someone: that person freezes, cannot move, cannot think of anything else, and is completely under the wizard's power. Now, "spellbound" borrows that image and uses it for real feelings in everyday life. You are not literally under a magic spell, but you feel as if you are — held in place by something so powerful and wonderful that you have no ability or desire to resist it.

So the word is built on a beautiful idea: when something truly mesmerizes you, it works like magic on your mind.

Anything extraordinary, beautiful, thrilling, or deeply impressive can leave someone spellbound. Common causes include:

A breathtaking musical performance. A stunning piece of art. A brilliant speech. A spectacular natural scene like a thunderstorm or a sunset over the ocean. A gripping story being told around a fire. A dancer moving in a way that seems physically impossible. A piece of writing so beautiful it stops you mid-sentence.

The key is that whatever caused it must feel remarkable — out of the ordinary. You do not become spellbound by something dull or routine.
How Deep and Intense Is This Feeling?

Spellbound sits at the strong end of the scale. It is more powerful than simply being "interested" or "impressed." Compare:

You might be interested in a documentary. You might be impressed by a good cooking show. But if you are spellbound, you are rooted to your seat, hanging on every word, barely breathing, fully captured. There is a sense of being held — as though an invisible force has taken hold of you and will not let go until the performance ends, the speech finishes, or the scene passes.

It is an intense, almost overwhelming absorption.

If you are the one who is spellbound, it feels like time slows down or disappears. Your surroundings fade. You are not aware of being tired, hungry, or distracted. You feel a kind of sweet, willing helplessness — you want to stay captured. There is often a sense of awe, wonder, or deep pleasure mixed in. It can feel almost dreamlike.

This is why spellbound almost always carries a positive, beautiful connotation. Being spellbound is not frightening or unpleasant — it is one of those rare, rich experiences where something in the world reaches out and grabs your entire being.
Can It Ever Be Used in a Slightly Negative Way?

Occasionally, spellbound can describe a state where the captivation is so strong it feels almost dangerous or suspicious — like someone being hypnotized by a con artist's charm, or a crowd being held in the grip of a manipulative speaker. In these rare cases, the "spell" idea becomes more literal and slightly sinister. But even then, the person who is spellbound is not suffering — they are simply unaware of the manipulation because they are too absorbed.

In everyday use, however, spellbound is almost always positive and warm.
How It Is Used in a Sentence (with Context)

Simple uses:

"The audience sat spellbound as the violinist played the final movement."
→ The audience was completely still and absorbed; no one moved or whispered.

"She had been spellbound by the Northern Lights, unable to move or speak for several minutes."
→ The natural spectacle had such a powerful effect on her that she was frozen in wonder.

"The children were spellbound by the old man's storytelling."
→ Every child was silent, wide-eyed, and fully absorbed — not a single one fidgeted.

More nuanced uses:

"He kept the entire conference room spellbound for an hour without a single slide."
→ His speaking alone — no visuals, no tools — was enough to hold everyone's complete attention. This suggests he was exceptionally gifted.

"She had a way of looking at you that left you spellbound, as though everything she said was the most important thing in the world."
→ Used here to describe a person's magnetic, captivating presence.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close cousins, but each has its own shade of meaning:

Fascinated — A broad word. You are curious and interested, but it is lighter and more mental. You can be fascinated while casually scrolling through an article. Spellbound is far more total and physical — your whole self is captured.

Captivated — Very similar to spellbound, but slightly less extreme. Captivated means your attention is held firmly and pleasurably. Spellbound suggests an even deeper, almost magical degree of that captivation.

Mesmerized — Very close to spellbound. Mesmerized often emphasizes the trance-like quality — your eyes are fixed, you are barely blinking, you are in a kind of daze. Spellbound has that same quality but also carries the extra warmth of wonder and delight.

Entranced — Similar to mesmerized, with a dreamlike feeling. Entranced leans into the idea of being in a trance. Spellbound leans into the idea of magic and complete hold.

Transfixed — This specifically emphasizes being frozen to the spot, unable to move. You can be transfixed by something shocking or frightening (a car crash, for example) — it does not have to be pleasant. Spellbound is almost always pleasant.

Of all these words, spellbound is the one that most strongly combines: total captivation + a sense of magic + a feeling of wonder + genuine pleasure.
If you ever forget the exact meaning, just remember the image: a magic spell has been cast on you. You are frozen, helpless, completely held — but you love every second of it. That is spellbound.

Spellbound means so deeply and completely captivated by something wonderful that you are unable to look away, think of anything else, or resist its hold on you — as though a magic spell has been cast.
14954: To spelunk means to explore caves, especially as a hobby or recreational activity.

When you spelunk, you go into natural underground caves — not tunnels built by humans, not mines, but wild, natural caverns carved by water, rock, and time — and you move through them, often by crawling, climbing, squeezing through tight gaps, wading through underground streams, and descending into dark pits.

It is not a casual stroll. Caves are dark, often wet, physically demanding, and potentially dangerous. So to spelunk is to deliberately choose to go into these environments and navigate them, usually for the thrill and adventure of it.
What the Activity Actually Looks Like

Picture this: you put on a helmet with a headlamp, wear old clothes you don't mind getting muddy, and you enter the mouth of a cave. From there, you might:

  • Crawl on your belly through a passage barely wide enough for your shoulders
  • Climb down a rope into a large underground chamber the size of a cathedral
  • Squeeze sideways through a crack in the rock
  • Wade through an underground stream in pitch darkness
  • Discover a room full of stalactites (rock formations hanging from the ceiling)

That entire experience — from entering the cave to navigating its depths — is what "spelunking" refers to.

• "We spent the weekend spelunking in the caves near the national park."
  • "She spelunked for the first time last summer and was immediately hooked."
  • "He spelunks every chance he gets — he's obsessed with underground caves."
  • "Spelunking in unfamiliar caves without a guide can be very dangerous."
  • "They plan to spelunk through the newly discovered cavern system next month."
The Noun Forms You'll Naturally Encounter

The word naturally comes with two nouns you'll keep seeing:

  • Spelunker — a person who spelunks. "She's an experienced spelunker."
  • Spelunking — the activity itself, used as a noun. "Spelunking requires good physical fitness."

These three words (spelunk, spelunker, spelunking) are really one family, and you'll often see all three used interchangeably depending on what part of speech is needed in the sentence.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Spelunk" has a slightly informal, hobbyist feel to it. It carries the sense of recreational adventure — something you do for fun, challenge, and the joy of exploration — rather than a professional or scientific mission.

Scientists who study caves professionally are typically called speleologists, and they study the geology, biology, and structure of caves. That is a formal, scientific word. "Spelunk," by contrast, is the word for the enthusiast — the person who does it because they love the adventure.
How It Differs From Just "Exploring a Cave"

You might wonder: isn't spelunking just "going into a cave"? Not quite. The word implies:

  1. Active navigation of a challenging environment — you're not just walking along a lit tourist path inside a cave. You're genuinely moving through raw, unimproved cave passages.
  2. A recreational or hobbyist intent — you're doing it for the experience, not because you have to.
  3. Some level of physical effort and adventure — crawling, climbing, squeezing, etc.

A tourist walking through a well-lit, paved cave attraction is not really spelunking. Someone belly-crawling through a muddy underground passage with a headlamp very much is.
A Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

If you've ever seen footage of explorers crawling through tight rock passages with headlamps, emerging into vast underground chambers filled with strange rock formations, and wading through underground rivers — that is spelunking. The word captures all of that in a single, vivid verb.

To spelunk = to explore a natural cave, especially as a hobby, often involving crawling, climbing, and navigating physically challenging underground passages in the dark.
14955:
A spendthrift is a person who spends money carelessly, wastefully, and without restraint — someone who throws money away freely, often spending far more than they can afford, and almost never thinking about the future.

The key idea is not simply that they spend money. Everyone spends money. The key is how they do it: recklessly, without thought, and in ways that are genuinely harmful to their own financial life.

Imagine someone who gets their paycheck on Friday. By Sunday, it is completely gone — spent on things they didn't truly need: expensive nights out, impulse purchases, gadgets, luxuries. Now they have nothing left for rent, food, or an emergency. That person is a spendthrift.

Or picture a person who wins a lottery and, within a few years, has nothing left to show for it — because they could never stop spending. That, too, is a spendthrift.
What makes someone a spendthrift — the core qualities

A true spendthrift has a combination of these qualities, not just one in isolation:

Wasteful spending. They don't just spend — they waste. They buy things with little real value or necessity, or they dramatically overpay for things, or they spend just for the thrill of it.

A lack of self-control. A spendthrift finds it very hard to hold back. When money is in their hands, it leaves quickly. Saving feels almost impossible for them.

No concern for the future. They live entirely in the financial present. There is no thought for emergencies, savings, retirement, or what happens when the money runs out.

A pattern, not a one-time event. This is important. Calling someone a spendthrift means this is their habitual way of living, not just one bad week of overspending. It is a deeply ingrained behavior.

"Spendthrift" is a word of disapproval and criticism. When you call someone a spendthrift, you are not merely describing their behavior — you are judging it as foolish and irresponsible. The word carries a clear negative charge. It suggests that the person's relationship with money is broken in a way that will eventually hurt them, if it hasn't already.
How it differs from similar ideas

A generous person also spends money freely, but on others, and thoughtfully, within their means. A spendthrift spends without wisdom, usually driven by impulse or desire, not by a kind heart.

A wealthy person who spends a lot is not automatically a spendthrift. If you can genuinely afford what you spend, it is not wasteful. A spendthrift is defined by reckless and uncontrolled spending — not the amount itself. Even a very rich person can be a spendthrift if they burn through money foolishly.

Someone who occasionally treats themselves is not a spendthrift. The word requires a consistent, ongoing pattern of irresponsible spending.

"Don't lend him money — he's a complete spendthrift. He'll have spent it all before the week is out."

"Despite earning a high salary for thirty years, she died with almost nothing in the bank. Her family always knew she was a spendthrift, but nobody realized just how bad it was."

"He tried hard not to become the spendthrift his father had been, so he started tracking every dollar he spent."

"The young heir was a notorious spendthrift — the entire family fortune was gone within a decade of him inheriting it."
A spendthrift is a person who habitually spends money foolishly, wastefully, and without self-control — and the word always carries a tone of criticism toward that behavior.
14956:
Spent means completely used up, with nothing left over. It describes the state of something — a person, an object, or even a force — after it has given or used everything it had. The key word here is completely. "Spent" doesn't mean half-empty or running low. It means the tank is at zero. Whatever power, energy, or usefulness it once held is now gone.

Think of it this way: when you "spend" money, you use it up and it leaves your hands. "Spent," as an adjective, captures that same idea — something has been fully used, and what remains is the empty shell of what it once was.
The Three Main Ways "Spent" Is Used

1. Describing a Person — Complete Exhaustion

When a person is described as "spent," it means they are totally drained. Not just tired or sleepy — but emptied of every last bit of energy, strength, or emotion. Their body or mind (or both) simply have nothing left to give. It is a deeper, more final-feeling word than "tired" or even "exhausted."

"After swimming forty laps, she pulled herself out of the pool and lay on the floor, completely spent."

"He had cried for hours. By midnight, he was spent — too empty to feel anything more."

Notice that "spent" fits situations where a person has pushed themselves to their absolute limit. There is often a quiet sense of having given everything.

2. Describing Objects — Used Up and Useless

When an object is "spent," it has been used up and can no longer perform its function. This is especially common in technical and formal language.

A spent bullet or spent cartridge is a bullet that has already been fired. The explosive inside it did its job, and what's left is just an empty metal casing — it cannot fire again.

Spent fuel (especially in the context of nuclear power) is fuel that has already been used in a reactor and can no longer generate power the way it once could.

A spent match is a match that has already been struck and burned. It cannot produce a flame again.

In all these cases, the object went through a process that used it up completely. It did its job. Now it is spent.

3. Describing a Force, Power, or Movement — Power That Has Run Out

"Spent" is also used for things like storms, rivers, emotions, or social/political movements — any kind of force that was once powerful but has exhausted itself.

"By the time the hurricane reached the mountains, it was spent — little more than a strong breeze."

"Many analysts believe that this political party is now a spent force."

The phrase "a spent force" is particularly common and worth remembering. It describes something — a person, an institution, a trend — that was once influential or powerful but has used up all its strength and no longer matters in the same way.

"Spent" carries a subtle emotional weight that its synonyms sometimes lack. When you call something "spent," you are quietly acknowledging that it gave everything it had. A spent soldier fought with full effort. A spent storm raged completely. There is a sense of finality, but also of something having been fully lived or fully used — not wasted, but exhausted through genuine effort or natural process.

This is what separates "spent" from a word like "empty." An empty bottle may never have had much in it. A spent one gave everything it contained.

Tired — A mild, temporary feeling of fatigue. You recover after rest. A tired person can still function.

Exhausted — Much stronger than tired. Very drained. But "exhausted" is mostly used for people and animals, and it still feels like something a good sleep might fix.

Spent — The deepest level. Completely used up. It applies not just to people, but to objects and forces too. When someone is "spent," they have been fully emptied — not just worn down. It also carries a sense of having already given everything, which "exhausted" doesn't always imply.

"Spent" as an adjective means completely used up, with nothing remaining. It can describe:

  • A person who is totally drained of energy or emotion.
  • An object (like a bullet or a match) that has been used and can no longer function.
  • A force or power (like a storm or a movement) that has exhausted itself and lost its strength.

The word always points to the same truth: whatever was there before — energy, power, usefulness — has been fully consumed. The process is complete. Nothing is left.
14957:
To spew means to pour or push something out forcefully, rapidly, in a large and uncontrolled amount — usually from an opening of some kind, like a mouth, a pipe, a vent, or a machine.

Think of a garden hose that suddenly bursts. Water doesn't drip out gently. It shoots out with force, fast, and in a big messy stream. That kind of forceful, out-of-control outpouring is exactly what spew captures.

Two qualities are almost always present when you use "spew":

  • Force — things don't leak or trickle; they shoot or pour out with energy.
  • Large quantity — there's a lot of whatever is coming out, not just a little.

And very often, a third quality appears:

  • Unpleasantness — what comes out is usually something bad, messy, or unwanted.

In its most concrete, physical sense, spew describes something real being forcefully expelled from an opening.

A volcano can spew lava, ash, and smoke. It doesn't politely release them — it shoots them out violently in huge amounts.

A factory chimney spews thick black smoke into the air. The image is of smoke billowing and pouring out aggressively, non-stop.

A damaged pipe might spew water all over the floor — not a slow drip, but a sudden, forceful gush.

A person can literally spew as well — it's a vivid, informal word for vomiting. "He felt so sick that he spewed his entire meal." It deliberately sounds more dramatic and unpleasant than the clinical word "vomit," which suits the ugliness of the situation.

In all these cases, the thing being spewed is coming out of something, in large amounts, without much control.

This is where "spew" becomes truly powerful and widely used in everyday English. It is very commonly applied to language, speech, and information — and this is always where a negative judgment is being made.

When a person spews words, they are saying a large amount of something bad, harmful, or worthless, rapidly and without much thought or restraint.

Consider these examples:

  • "The politician spewed lies for an hour."

This means the politician said a large number of lies, one after another, fast and relentlessly — like a machine pouring out garbage.

  • "He just spews insults whenever he's angry."

He doesn't carefully choose one insult. He throws out a flood of them, out of control.

  • "That website spews misinformation."

The website produces a huge and constant stream of false information.

Notice what spew does here that words like "say" or "talk" don't do: it communicates that the speaker thinks what's being said is worthless, harmful, or disgusting — just like smoke or vomit. It is a loaded word. Simply by choosing "spew," you are telling the reader that you disapprove of what is being said and that you find it excessive and offensive.

You would never say "She spewed brilliant ideas" — that would sound very wrong, because spew almost always carries a negative feeling. It's reserved for things the speaker finds repulsive or objectionable.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Spew is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a tone of disgust, criticism, or alarm. When a writer or speaker uses "spew," they are signaling one or more of these feelings:

  • Disgust — what's coming out is foul or unwanted.
  • Disapproval — the person or thing doing the spewing has no restraint or care.
  • Alarm — the sheer volume and force of it is overwhelming or dangerous.

This makes "spew" a very expressive and colorful word. It paints a strong picture quickly. A sentence like "The speaker spewed hatred at the crowd" is far more powerful than "The speaker said hateful things to the crowd."
How Spew Differs From Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it differs from its neighbors:

Spew vs. Pour — "Pour" is generally neutral and can even be positive (pour a glass of wine). Spew is almost never positive, and it always suggests mess and lack of control.

Spew vs. Emit — "Emit" is a calm, technical word (the device emits a signal). Spew is dramatic, excessive, and unpleasant. A machine emits exhaust; a broken, overheated one spews it.

Spew vs. Gush — "Gush" can be positive (she gushed about how much she loved the film). Spew cannot be positive. Both involve force and large quantity, but gush can express enthusiasm while spew expresses disgust.

Spew vs. Vomit — As a figurative verb for speech, "vomit" works similarly (he vomited insults), but it is slightly more extreme and rarer. Spew feels more natural in everyday speech for this figurative use.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Spew = to expel something forcefully, in large and uncontrolled amounts, usually from an opening — whether that something is a physical substance (lava, smoke, water, vomit) or words and ideas (lies, insults, propaganda). The word almost always suggests the thing being expelled is unwanted, harmful, or disgusting, and that it's coming out with too much force and in too great a quantity to be considered acceptable.

If you remember just one image: a volcano erupting — powerful, out of control, releasing a massive amount of something dangerous. That is the spirit of "spew" in every context it's used.

A sphere is a perfectly round, three-dimensional shape in which every single point on its surface is exactly the same distance from the center. That fixed distance is called the radius.

Think of a marble, a soap bubble, or a ball bearing. Every point on their surface is equidistant from the middle. That is the defining quality of a sphere — not just roundness, but perfect roundness in all directions simultaneously.

This is important: a sphere is not flat. A circle is the flat, two-dimensional cousin of a sphere. Draw a circle on paper — it has no depth. Now imagine inflating it in every direction outward until it becomes a ball. That ball is a sphere. It has length, width, and depth. It occupies real space.

In mathematics and geometry, a sphere is defined with precision. The surface of a sphere is the shell — the outer skin of the ball shape. The space inside that shell is technically called a ball in advanced mathematics, though in everyday life people use "sphere" to mean the whole solid object, and that is perfectly fine.

A sphere has no edges, no corners, and no flat faces. It is the same shape from every angle. If you spin a sphere in any direction, it looks identical. Mathematicians call this property perfect symmetry.

Real-world examples of near-perfect spheres include soap bubbles, ball bearings, planets (roughly), and marbles. The Earth, for instance, is almost a sphere, but it bulges slightly at the equator, so scientists call it an oblate spheroid — a squashed sphere. The Sun and the Moon are also very close to being true spheres.

"Sphere" is also used to refer to any actual physical object that has that shape. You might hear someone say "a crystal sphere," "a hollow metal sphere," or "a glass sphere." Here, the word simply names the object itself — a thing shaped like a ball.

This is where the word becomes rich and widely used in everyday language.

A field or area of activity, knowledge, or interest. When someone says "that falls outside my sphere of expertise," they mean it is outside the area of knowledge they have mastered. Just as a geometric sphere has a defined boundary — its surface — a person's "sphere" of knowledge has limits too. The word captures the idea of a domain with boundaries. Other examples: "She works in the sphere of public health." "This question belongs to the sphere of philosophy, not science."

A sphere of influence. This is a very common phrase in politics, history, and international relations. It refers to the region, group of people, or area over which a person, organization, or country has significant power, control, or dominance — even if that control is informal. For example, during the Cold War, Eastern Europe was considered to be within the Soviet Union's sphere of influence, meaning the USSR had great control over those countries. A business leader might have a sphere of influence over an entire industry. A popular teacher might have a sphere of influence over hundreds of students.

A social world or social circle. "Sphere" can refer to the social environment a person inhabits — the world of people, institutions, and norms they live within. "They move in very different spheres" means two people belong to very different social worlds — perhaps one is an artist in a bohemian community, and the other is a corporate banker. Their lives, social contacts, and environments barely overlap. This usage treats society as divided into distinct "worlds" or domains, each like its own sphere.

A person's proper domain or place. In older and more formal usage, "sphere" referred to the particular role or position a person was expected to occupy — often used when talking about social class or gender roles in historical contexts. The phrase "know your sphere" once meant "know your place in the social order." This usage is largely outdated but you will encounter it in older literature.

In astronomy, the celestial sphere is an imaginary, infinitely large sphere surrounding the Earth. Ancient and medieval astronomers imagined all the stars as being fixed onto the inner surface of this great sphere, which rotated around the Earth. Even today, astronomers use the concept of the celestial sphere as a practical tool for mapping the sky and tracking the positions of stars, even though we now know the stars are not actually fixed on any surface.

In earth and environmental science, the word "sphere" is used to name the major systems of the planet. The atmosphere is the sphere of gases surrounding Earth. The hydrosphere is the sphere of all water — oceans, rivers, ice caps, groundwater. The lithosphere is the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth. The biosphere is the sphere of all living things. In each case, the word "sphere" conveys the idea of a distinct, globe-like layer or system that wraps around the planet.

Whether the word is used literally or figuratively, the concept of a sphere always carries the same underlying idea: a self-contained, bounded, rounded whole. Geometrically, it is a shape with a defined center and a perfectly even surface. Figuratively, it is a domain — of knowledge, power, influence, or social life — with its own center and its own limits.

So when you encounter the word "sphere" anywhere — in a math textbook, a political article, a history book, or a novel — ask yourself: is it describing a shape, a physical object, a field of activity, a zone of power, or a social world? The answer will almost always fit neatly into one of those categories, and the core idea of a bounded, rounded domain will always be present beneath the surface.
14959: Spherical simply means shaped like a sphere — that is, perfectly round in three dimensions, like a ball. If something is spherical, it has no flat sides, no corners, no edges. It curves smoothly all the way around, and no matter which direction you look at it from, it looks like a circle.
What exactly is a sphere?

A sphere is a perfectly round solid shape in three-dimensional space. The defining rule of a sphere is this: every single point on its surface is exactly the same distance from its center. That distance is called the radius.

Think of a ball of clay. If you could measure from the very center of the ball to any point on its outer surface — top, bottom, left side, right side, any point at all — the distance would always be identical. That's what makes it a sphere, and that's what "spherical" means when it describes the shape of something.
How spherical differs from circular

This is an important distinction many learners miss.

A circle is flat — it exists in two dimensions (length and width). It's just a ring or a disk.

A sphere is three-dimensional — it has length, width, and depth (or height). It has volume inside it.

So:

  • A coin is circular (flat, 2D).
  • A ball is spherical (round in all directions, 3D).

The word "spherical" always implies three-dimensional roundness. Never flat.
Perfectly spherical vs. approximately spherical

In strict geometric terms, a perfect sphere is an idealized, mathematical object. In the real world, almost nothing is perfectly spherical — there are always tiny imperfections.

For this reason, you'll often see the word used with qualifiers:

  • "nearly spherical" — very close to a sphere, but not perfect
  • "approximately spherical" — roughly sphere-shaped for practical purposes
  • "almost perfectly spherical" — extremely close, with only tiny deviations

For example, the Earth is not perfectly spherical — it bulges slightly at the equator and is flattened a little at the poles. Scientists describe it as an oblate spheroid (a squashed sphere). But for most everyday purposes, we still call it spherical because it's close enough.

A soap bubble, on the other hand, comes remarkably close to a perfect sphere because surface tension pulls it uniformly inward from all directions.
Everyday examples

These objects are described as spherical (or approximately spherical):

  • A basketball, tennis ball, golf ball
  • A marble
  • A soap bubble
  • Planets and stars (including the Sun and Earth)
  • A round Christmas ornament
  • A ball bearing (the tiny steel balls inside machines)
  • A water droplet floating in zero gravity
  • An orange (roughly spherical, though slightly bumpy)
Where the word is used — different fields and contexts
1. Everyday language
The most common use is simply to describe the shape of an object. "The sculpture had a spherical shape." "The fruit was small and spherical."
2. Mathematics and geometry

In geometry, "spherical" is used to describe concepts that belong to or take place on the surface of a sphere. For example:

  • Spherical geometry is the study of shapes and angles drawn on the surface of a sphere (which behaves differently from flat geometry — for instance, the angles of a triangle on a sphere can add up to more than 180°).
  • Spherical coordinates are a way of locating a point in 3D space using a radius and two angles, instead of the usual x, y, z system.
  • A spherical triangle is a triangle drawn on the surface of a sphere, where the sides are arcs of great circles.
3. Astronomy

Historically, astronomers talked about "celestial spheres" — the idea that stars and planets were embedded in invisible rotating spheres around the Earth. Terms like spherical astronomy and the celestial sphere (an imaginary giant sphere around Earth on which stars appear projected) come from this.

Today, planets, moons, and stars are described as spherical because gravity naturally pulls matter into the most compact shape possible — a sphere.
4. Optics and physics

• A spherical lens is a lens whose curved surface is part of a sphere. Most ordinary eyeglass lenses and camera lenses are spherical lenses.
  • A spherical mirror is a mirror whose reflecting surface is a portion of a sphere — either curved inward (concave) or outward (convex). Concave spherical mirrors can focus light; convex ones spread it (like the wide-angle mirrors in parking lots).
  • Spherical aberration is a flaw in lenses or mirrors where light hitting the outer edges doesn't focus at the same point as light hitting the center — a defect because of the spherical shape.
5. Navigation and geography

Since the Earth is approximately spherical, navigation uses spherical trigonometry — mathematics designed specifically for calculating distances and angles on a sphere. This is how pilots and sailors calculate the shortest route between two points on the globe (called a great-circle route).
A subtle but important point: "spherical" vs. "round"

In everyday speech, people use "round" loosely to mean many things — a circle, a sphere, a cylinder, an oval. "Spherical" is more precise. It specifically means three-dimensionally round in every direction, with every surface point equidistant from the center. So while a cylinder (like a can) is "round," it is not spherical — it has flat ends and straight sides. "Spherical" rules out any such flatness or straightness.
How it's used grammatically

As an adjective, "spherical" directly describes a noun:

  • "The room had a spherical lamp hanging from the ceiling."
  • "The droplets became spherical as they fell."
  • "Scientists confirmed the asteroid was surprisingly spherical."

It can also appear after a linking verb:

  • "The shape of the bubble was perfectly spherical."
Summary

Spherical means: perfectly round in three dimensions, shaped like a sphere, where every point on the outer surface is the same distance from the center.

It implies complete, all-around roundness — no flat faces, no corners, no uneven bulges. In everyday use, it describes ball-shaped objects. In technical fields like geometry, physics, astronomy, and optics, it refers to anything that belongs to, is derived from, or behaves like a sphere. When precision matters, something is spherical only if it truly (or approximately) satisfies that geometric condition of uniform distance from the center.
